mainTopic: When a sold item turns out unfit for the buyer's purpose: seeds that do not sprout (משנה) and an ox that gores (רב and שמואל)
overview: The משנה rules that someone who sells produce that did not sprout is not responsible, because the buyer might have bought it to eat. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל disagrees about garden seeds, which nobody eats, so the seller is responsible for them. The גמרא then brings a related argument: if someone sells an ox that turns out to be a gorer, רב says the sale is a mistake, and שמואל says the seller can claim he sold it for slaughter. The גמרא asks why we do not just check what this buyer usually buys oxen for, and answers that he buys them for both purposes. It then asks why we do not check the price he paid, and answers that meat prices rose until a meat ox cost as much as a plowing ox. If the prices are equal, what difference does the argument make? The גמרא answers that it decides who must take on the effort of selling the ox. The amud ends as the גמרא asks to define the exact case, and the answer comes on the next amud.

steps.title: Seller of produce that did not sprout is not responsible
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא rules that a seller of produce is not liable if the buyer planted it and it failed to grow, even for flaxseed.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone sells produce to another person, and the buyer plants it and it does not sprout, the seller does not have to pay him back. This is true even for flaxseed.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a rule: a seller does not have to pay if the seeds he sold did not grow. This holds even for flaxseed, which people mostly plant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Produce can be bought to eat or to plant. The buyer never said he wanted to plant it, so the seller can say, 'I assumed you would eat it.' The word 'even' tells us the rule still holds for flaxseed, which is only sometimes eaten.

keyTerms.meaning: Produce; here, crops that can be eaten or planted
They sprouted (here: they did NOT sprout)
Flaxseed
Responsibility; the seller's duty to pay if something goes wrong

phrases.english: One who sells produce to his fellow,
and he planted them and they did not sprout;
and even flaxseed –
phrases.notes: Flaxseed is usually planted and only sometimes eaten, so you might have thought the seller should pay here.

phrases.english: he is not responsible for them.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A seller of produce is not liable if the buyer planted it and it did not sprout, even for flaxseed, since the buyer may have intended to eat it.

steps.title: Garden seeds that are not eaten carry responsibility
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says that for garden seeds nobody eats, the seller is responsible.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: for garden seeds that are not eaten, the seller is responsible.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל gives a different rule for seeds that people never eat. In that case the seller must pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason the seller could escape in step 1 was that the buyer might have meant to eat the seeds. Garden seeds are not food, so the only reason to buy them is to plant them. That excuse is gone, and the seller is responsible.

keyTerms.meaning: Garden seeds
Eaten

steps.whatToRemember: The whole question is: what was the item bought for? If it could be food, the seller can say 'I sold it to eat.' If it is only for planting, the seller is responsible.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
garden seeds that are not eaten,
he is responsible for them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a dissenting view for seeds that can only be planted.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For garden seeds that are not eaten, the seller bears responsibility, because they were surely bought for planting.

steps.title: רב and שמואל argue about selling an ox that gores
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings an argument: if a sold ox turns out to gore, רב says the sale is a mistake, and שמואל says the seller can claim it was sold for slaughter.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was said: if someone sells an ox and it turns out to be a gorer, רב says the sale is a mistaken sale. שמואל says the seller can tell the buyer, 'I sold it to you for slaughter.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a disagreement between רב and שמואל about a sold ox that turns out to gore. It is a similar question to the משנה: what was the item bought for?
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ox can be bought to plow or to slaughter for meat. A goring ox is useless for plowing but fine for meat. רב lets the buyer say 'I bought it to plow,' so the sale is undone. שמואל lets the seller say 'I sold it for meat,' so the sale stands.

keyTerms.meaning: An ox that habitually gores
A mistaken sale; the sale is undone and the money returned
For slaughter

steps.confusionAlert: שמואל is not saying the buyer actually bought it for meat. He is saying the seller is allowed to make that claim, so the buyer cannot prove the sale was a mistake.
steps.whyThisMatters: This argument becomes the focus of the rest of the סוגיא, and the גמרא will try to tie it to our משנה about seeds.

phrases.english: GEMARA: It was stated:
one who sells an ox to his fellow
and it is found to be a gorer,

phrases.aramaic: רַב אָמַר: הֲרֵי זֶה מִקָּח טָעוּת;
phrases.english: Rav says: this is a mistaken sale;
and Shmuel says: he can say to him:
phrases.notes: 'He' is the seller, speaking to the buyer.

phrases.english: I sold it to you for slaughter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a similar case (an ox with more than one possible use) alongside the משנה's seed case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: a goring ox sale is a mistaken sale. שמואל: the seller can claim he sold it for slaughter, so the sale stands.

steps.title: Why not check what this buyer usually buys oxen for?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: just look at the buyer's habits. If he buys for slaughter, it was for slaughter; if for plowing, it was for plowing.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us look! If he is a man who buys oxen for slaughter, then this was for slaughter. If he buys for plowing, then this was for plowing!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why there is any argument at all. We could simply check what this buyer normally does with the oxen he buys.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument between רב and שמואל depends on not knowing why the ox was bought. The גמרא points out that the buyer's usual habit should tell us. If so, there would be no reason to argue.

keyTerms.meaning: But let us see; let us check
Slaughter (for meat)
Plowing

phrases.english: But let us see;
if he is a man who buys for slaughter – it was for slaughter,
if for plowing – it was for plowing!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the argument in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The argument between רב and שמואל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The buyer's usual habit should reveal his purpose, so there should be nothing to argue about.

steps.title: The buyer buys oxen for both purposes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the argument is about a buyer who sometimes buys for slaughter and sometimes for plowing.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is a man who buys oxen for this and for that.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by saying the buyer has no single habit. He buys oxen for both uses, so his habit tells us nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Checking habits only helps when the buyer has a clear pattern. Here he does both, so we really do not know why he bought this ox. That is why רב and שמואל can argue.

keyTerms.meaning: For this and for that; for both purposes

phrases.english: It is about a man who buys for this and for that.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 4 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We could have checked the buyer's habit to know his purpose.
steps.terutzMaskana: The argument is about a buyer with no fixed habit, so his purpose is truly unknown.

steps.title: Why not check the price that was paid?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges again: look at the price, since a plowing ox costs more than an ox for meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us see what the price was!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks another question: the price the buyer paid should show what he wanted the ox for. The next step answers this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the buyer's habit does not help, the price might. An ox fit for plowing costs more than one only good for meat. If he paid the plowing price, his purpose would be clear, and again there would be nothing to argue about.

keyTerms.meaning: The price; the money paid
How much is it? What is it like?

phrases.english: But let us see the price, how much it was!
phrases.notes: A plowing ox costs more than one only good for meat, so the price would show his purpose.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Even after the answer in step 5, raises a new way to find the buyer's purpose.
steps.kashyaTarget: The argument between רב and שמואל, even for a buyer who buys for both purposes
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The price paid shows whether the ox was bought for plowing or for meat, so the buyer's purpose should be known.

steps.title: The price of meat went up to match a plowing ox
steps.stepSummary: The argument is about a time when meat prices rose so high that a meat ox cost the same as a plowing ox. So the price cannot tell us what the לוקח wanted.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the case is needed where meat became expensive, and a meat ox reached the price of a plowing ox.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 6, which said we could just look at the price. It explains that in this case both kinds of oxen cost the same, so the price gives no clue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually a plowing ox costs more than a meat ox, so the price would show what the לוקח meant to buy. But here meat prices went up until both kinds cost the same. Now neither the לוקח's habits nor the price can tell us anything, and that is why רב and שמואל argue.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not needed (except for...): the case is really talking about a special situation
It became expensive / went up in price
Meat
Reached the price of / stood at the value of

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the גמרא means meat oxen are always as expensive as plowing oxen. This is a special time when meat prices rose. Normally a plowing ox costs more.

phrases.english: No, it is needed where meat became expensive,
and it reached the price of a plowing ox.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the price challenge of Step 6 by narrowing the case to one where the prices are equal.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא) to a situation where the challenge's clue does not work
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the price would always show whether the ox was bought for meat or for plowing.
steps.terutzMaskana: The argument is about a time when meat prices rose to match plowing prices, so price proves nothing.

steps.title: If the prices are the same, what difference does it make?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if both oxen cost the same, the לוקח loses no money either way, so why does the argument matter?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what practical difference is there?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from Step 7. If the gorer is worth the same as a plowing ox, it seems nobody really loses anything.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The לוקח wanted a plowing ox but got a gorer that is only good for meat. But if meat oxen now cost the same as plowing oxen, he can sell it for meat and get all his money back. So whether the sale is a mistake (רב) or not (שמואל) seems to make no difference.

keyTerms.meaning: If so: if what you just said is true
For what?
Practical difference / what comes out of it

phrases.english: If so, for what is there a practical difference?
phrases.notes: The point: he can sell the ox for meat at full price, so who cares whether the sale stands?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of Step 7: narrowing the case to equal prices seems to empty the argument of any real result.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in Step 7 that the argument is about a time when meat and plowing oxen cost the same.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the prices are equal, the לוקח loses no money no matter who is right, so the argument between רב and שמואל would have no practical effect.

steps.title: The difference is who has to bother selling the ox
steps.stepSummary: Even if no money is lost, someone has to go to the trouble of selling the ox. The argument decides whether that is the מוכר or the לוקח.
steps.simpleTranslation: The practical difference is the effort.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 8. It explains that the argument really matters for the work and bother of selling the ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב, the sale is a mistake, so the לוקח gives the ox back and the מוכר has to deal with selling it. According to שמואל, the sale stands, so the לוקח has to go sell the gorer for meat himself. The money is the same either way, but the effort falls on a different person.

keyTerms.meaning: Effort, bother, trouble

steps.whatToRemember: Even when no money is at stake, the רב and שמואל argument still matters: it decides who must take on the טרחא of selling the gorer.
steps.whyThisMatters: This teaches that a halachic argument can have a real result even without any money loss. Who has to do the work counts too.

phrases.english: The practical difference is with regard to the effort.
phrases.notes: He means the effort of selling the ox again to get the money back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 8 by naming a practical result that is not about money.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing a different practical result (נפקא מינה) that the challenge did not consider
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought that if no money is lost, the argument has no real effect.
steps.terutzMaskana: The argument decides who must take on the effort of selling the ox: the מוכר according to רב, the לוקח according to שמואל.

steps.title: What exactly is the case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the exact situation it is talking about. This sets up the next part of the discussion.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא is asking to define the exact case, and the answer comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the גמרא has narrowed the case several times: a לוקח with mixed habits, and equal prices. Now it asks to pin down the full picture of the case before it continues. The answer comes on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: What are the circumstances? What does the case look like?

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After settling the practical difference in Step 9, the גמרא now asks to define the exact case it is talking about.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact situation in which the argument between רב and שמואל applies.
